video:video.video:title: Cânticos de Silício I
video:video.video:description: Cânticos de Silício I is the first work in which I used the OpenScofo system, an AI capable of synchronizing the computer and the performer. The name Cânticos de Silício (something like Silicon Chants) comes from the idea of a work that allows the sounds of the concretization of the artifact to emerge. In this particular piece, created for my PhD, trill detection needed to work for OpenScofo. Since I was studying this, I decided to make a work specifically to put the system to the test.

video:video.video:title: Eco I
video:video.video:description: Eco I explores a feedback loop where sounds are analyzed through a continuously updated Fourier Transform, converted into musical scores, and reinterpreted by performers. An algorithm guides them to microtonal adjustments beyond the tempered scale, creating evolving harmonies that merge analysis and performance, with moments of consonance inspired by Harry Partch’s Just Intonation.

video:video.video:title: Estudo Microtonal no. 4
video:video.video:description: A work for flute and electronics, premiered by Denusa Castellain. In addition to Max/MSP, the piece uses Arshia Cont’s Antescofo software. This is the first piece in which I employ live electronics and just intonation.

video:video.video:title: Estudo Microtonal no. 5
video:video.video:description: A study piece exploring the concept of an Open Work. The pitches generated by the electronics are determined randomly, producing ever-changing, unpredictable textures.

video:video.video:title: Ideias Roubadas II
video:video.video:description: This piece is using the idea of the Meta-Instrument. It is based on the idea of transforming the guitar of the composer Arthur Kampela. I also use Luiza, by Tom Jobim. The idea of arranging the piece with contemporary techniques comes from Prof. Luiz Castelões.

video:video.video:title: Ideias Roubadas III
video:video.video:description: Ideias Roubadas III is a work inspired by the proposal of the UPIC system, developed by Iannis Xenakis in collaboration with the Centre d'Etudes de Mathématique et Automatique Musicales (CEMAMu) in Paris. Like UPIC, this piece employs an approach that manipulates visual elements to generate music using PureData to render the audio. I employ the concept of instruments (inspired by Csound) to render the sounds. Each color represents a sound or a set of instructions for spacialization, envelope, and others.

video:video.video:title: Metamorfose Inexata
video:video.video:description: In this work, I explore the idea of transposition between different tuning systems using notes that are very similar across these systems. This approach was described by composer Ben Johnston and is extensively employed in his string quartets.

video:video.video:title: Moteto
video:video.video:description: In this work, sound feedback is mediated through a continuously updating Fourier Transform, converting performed pitches into new scores. The choir receives this feedback through headphones and recreates microtonal tunings guided by these pitches, forming dynamic cycles where notes, FFT analysis, and justly tuned chords interact.

video:video.video:title: Nis
video:video.video:description: NIS emerges from a world shaped by mobile devices, where the smartphone functions as an extension of attention and the body. Developed within an ongoing postdoctoral research project supervised by Cássia Carrascoza, the work explores sound interaction in digital and performative environments through real-time algorithmic spatialization driven by motion sensors and mobile-device compasses. The piece investigates how technological mediation influences movement, performative decisions, and shared listening, creating an experience in which listening, movement, and technology operate simultaneously.
